voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
Because the life we speak of was lived as one body, under one shepherd, answerable for one another. When the imperial order came down, some bought the paper without making the sacrifice. Cyprian said their hands were clean but their conscience was not. That was not one person's private trouble. It was a wound in the body, and a bishop carried it as his own. When Cyprian himself was sentenced, the record tells what happened next. The Acta Proconsularia of Cyprian records: “After this sentence the crowd of the brothers kept saying, ‘Let us be beheaded with him too.’ Because of this an uproar rose among the brothers, and a large crowd followed him.”

They did not watch a stranger die for an idea. They saw their own shepherd taken, and they were his flock. We say we because that is what we were. Augustine told his own people the same thing in a different way, teaching them to pray. What you do, God does in you. That is not the voice of an isolated believer standing alone before God. It is a body that moves together, under one head. We say we because there was no other word for what held us.

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: Cyprian uses the word himself, in De Lapsis and in his letter to Antonianus. The English translation renders libelli as certificates, so the Latin headword is absent from the vendored English volume apart from one occurrence in the Introductory Notice to the anonymous treatise against Novatian. The Latin witnesses carry it. Latin libellus in Cyprian also names the martyrs' petitions, so the split between this term and lpc.term.certificates-letters-of-peace separates the English word and is not a distinction the Latin makes.
